items.working: Solar relates to the Sun; lunar relates to the Moon.
semanticFlags: stock textbook analogy
items.originalityNote: SOLAR:SUN::LUNAR:MOON is a canonical analogy found in many practice books.
items.notes: Relabel easy. Consider a fresher adjective pair (e.g. AQUATIC:WATER::ARBOREAL:?) if originality matters.

items.working: An author creates a novel; a composer creates a symphony.
items.notes: Relabel easy. ORCHESTRA is a fair distractor (performs, not creates).

items.working: A scalpel is the tool a surgeon uses; a chisel is the tool a sculptor uses.
semanticFlags: CARPENTRY is a trade, not a person, so it is ruled out only by part of speech; carpenters also use chisels
items.notes: Fine. CARPENTRY is a good part-of-speech trap; keep it as a noun of activity, not CARPENTER.

items.working: A drought is a severe lack of rainfall; a famine is a severe lack of food.
semanticFlags: HUNGER is a strong consequence-based distractor, but the lack-of relation selects FOOD only

items.working: A petal is a part of a flower; a tine is a prong/part of a fork.
semanticFlags: relies on knowing TINE; that is the point of the item
items.originalityNote: Part:whole analogy with a vocabulary hook.

items.working: An aviary houses birds; an apiary houses bees.
semanticFlags: stock analogy
items.originalityNote: AVIARY:BIRDS::APIARY:BEES is a very well-known vocabulary analogy in selective-test prep.
items.notes: Acceptable but stock; ANTS is a good near-miss distractor.

items.working: Arid and moist are opposites; the opposite of frail is sturdy.
semanticFlags: ARID's usual opposite is WET/HUMID; MOIST is acceptable
items.notes: Relabel easy; all distractors are synonyms of FRAIL so the antonym stands out immediately.

items.working: Triangle, hexagon, pentagon, octagon are 2D polygons; a cylinder is a 3D solid with curved surfaces.
semanticFlags: trivially easy; prompt says 'geometric shapes'
items.notes: Relabel easy, or swap CYLINDER for a subtler odd one out (e.g. CIRCLE, not a polygon).

items.working: Dolphin is a mammal; sardine, snapper, tuna and mackerel are fish.
semanticFlags: secondary reading: SNAPPER is the only non-oily fish, but the mammal reading is far stronger
items.originalityNote: Dolphin-is-a-mammal odd-one-out is a stock puzzle.

items.working: A barometer is a weather instrument, not a work of art.
semanticFlags: prompt gives the answer away by stating 'the other four works of art'
PORTRAIT is a subject genre while the others are media/forms (minor)
items.notes: Change prompt to 'Which word does NOT belong with the others?' and replace BAROMETER with a subtler intruder (e.g. EASEL - art-related but not a work of art).

items.working: Dwindle, recede, diminish, decline all mean to lessen/go down; prosper means to thrive.
Copper is a pure element; bronze, brass, steel and pewter are alloys.
semanticFlags: relies on science knowledge (alloys) and PEWTER vocabulary rather than pure verbal reasoning
items.originalityNote: Alloy odd-one-out appears in quiz books but content is fresh enough.
items.notes: Either relabel hard or move to a general-knowledge strand; some Year 6 students will not know pewter or brass composition.

items.working: Canberra, Wellington, Ottawa and London are national capitals; Sydney is not.
semanticFlags: general-knowledge dependent; slight culture bias toward Commonwealth geography
'status' is vague wording
items.originalityNote: Capital-city odd-one-out, Sydney/Canberra trap is common in Australian materials.
items.notes: Wording 'status' is vague but naming 'capital' would give it away; acceptable. Relabel easy.

items.working: Cautious = careful = prudent.
Conceal = hide; opposite is disclose (reveal).
Vigorous = energetic.
semanticFlags: LETHARGIC is the antonym trap

items.working: Scarcity = shortage; opposite = abundance.
Revered = deeply respected = esteemed.
semanticFlags: FEARED is a plausible awe-related distractor but clearly weaker

items.working: Divergent (moving apart) vs convergent (coming together).
semanticFlags: answer can be found by morphology alone (DI-/CON- + VERGENT) without knowing meaning
items.notes: Replace CONVERGENT with a non-cognate antonym such as SIMILAR/UNIFORM, or keep it but relabel easy.

items.working: Apprehensive = worried/anxious.
items.notes: Good; EAGER is a nice trap.

items.working: NEWSPAPER and PAPERWEIGHT; NEWSPRINT works but PRINTWEIGHT does not; NEWSFLASH/NEWSDESK work but FLASHWEIGHT/DESKWEIGHT do not.
items.notes: Good; three distractors satisfy the first half, which is good design.

items.working: BLOCK = a building block (e.g. concrete block) and = to obstruct.
semanticFlags: the first definition describes BRICK more naturally than BLOCK, and 'to brick (up)' can mean to seal/obstruct, so BRICK is a weak second reading
items.notes: Tighten definition 1 to 'a solid cube or chunk, e.g. of wood or ice' so BRICK is not attractive, or keep as intended trap after confirming 'brick' verb sense is not defensible.

items.working: POST = an upright wooden pole in a fence; POST = mail service (Australia Post).
semanticFlags: 'wooden boundary fence' is inaccurate - a post is part of a fence, not a fence
RAIL is also part of a fence
items.notes: Reword to 'an upright wooden pole, as in a fence' and 'the mail delivery service'.

items.working: SPADE = digging tool and card suit.
semanticFlags: stock homonym
items.originalityNote: Spade/suit homonym is a very common practice item.

items.working: BEAR = tolerate (can't bear it) and a large forest mammal.
semanticFlags: stock homonym; STAG/BOAR also fit the mammal half (intentional), STAND fits the verb half (intentional)
items.originalityNote: Bear/bear is a canonical homonym puzzle.

items.working: SUNLIGHT and LIGHTHOUSE; SUNSHINE/SUNSET/SUNDIAL/SUNBURST fail the second half.
semanticFlags: stock (lighthouse)

items.working: Whales are mammals; mammals breathe air; so all whales breathe air.
semanticFlags: B and E are converse-error traps

items.working: Modus tollens: if snow then early opening; not early opening, so no snow.
semanticFlags: note: real-world reading (trail could fail to open for other reasons even after snow) is excluded by the premise; fine

items.working: Every chess team student wears a blue badge; Anika is on the team; so Anika wears one.
semanticFlags: near-duplicate structure of 027/030/031

items.working: All brass instruments need air; a trumpet is brass; so it needs air.
semanticFlags: near-duplicate of 029/031 (modus ponens); distractors B/C/E are absurd and give no challenge
items.notes: Vary the logic form (e.g. 'Some...', or an affirming-the-consequent trap as the most attractive distractor) and replace absurd distractors.

items.working: Raptors have sharp talons; osprey is a raptor; so osprey has sharp talons.
semanticFlags: third consecutive modus-ponens item; 'possesses' slightly formal
items.notes: Convert to a harder form (e.g. 'A bird has sharp talons. Must it be a raptor?') to test converse error.

items.working: Modus tollens: lawn not wet, so sprinkler did not run.
semanticFlags: structure duplicates 028

items.working: +3 each step: B,E,H,K,N.
-2 each step: Z,X,V,T,R.
Positions 1,4,9,16 are squares; next 25 = Y.
items.notes: Relabel hard (or keep medium-hard); a solid discriminating item.

items.working: First letter +1 (E), second letter -1 (V): EV.
+4 each step: C,G,K,O,S.
Consecutive alternate letters: AC EG IK MO QS (+4 per pair, each pair skips one).
23,26,3,6 (+3 wrapping round), next 9 = I.
semanticFlags: 'modular' is unfamiliar jargon for Year 6 and gives away the wrap-around hint
items.notes: Remove the word 'modular'; let students discover the wrap-around.

items.working: +2: L->N, E->G, A->C, F->H = NGCH.
semanticFlags: prompt states the rule '(each letter shifted forward by 2)', removing the reasoning step
items.notes: Delete the parenthetical rule so students must infer it from BARK -> DCTM.

items.working: COLD->EQNF is +2; decode VJG by -2: T,H,E = THE.
items.notes: Good; decoding direction adds a step.

items.working: Letter substitution: P->J, O->W, S->K, T->D (consistent across both words). STOP -> K,D,W,J = KDWJ.
semanticFlags: LAMP is redundant except to confirm P->J; fine
items.notes: Good; distractors are permutations, which tests careful mapping.

items.working: Reverse BRIGHT: T,H,G,I,R,B = THGIRB.
items.notes: Relabel easy; distractors are good transposition traps.

packetSummary: All 45 items have exactly one defensible answer on my independent solve; 022 has a weak secondary BRICK reading. Main systemic issue: every item is labelled medium, but about 26 are easy for a strong Year 6 student (simple +n series, A1Z26 codes, modus ponens syllogisms, transparent synonyms); 012 and 035 are hard. Content revisions: 010 (prompt gives answer away), 040 (rule stated in prompt), 039 ('modular' hint), 019 (morphology gives answer), 023 (post is not a fence), 022 (definition fits BRICK), 012 (science-knowledge dependent), 030/031 (repetitive modus ponens with absurd distractors). Stock/near-canonical: 001, 006, 009, 024, 025. Counts: {"approve": 36, "revise": 9}
